notes.title: Monday Musings #25 – Bestagon Blueprints
notes.content:
The community has spoken loud and clear, and the time for Blueprints is here! Even though I knew this day would always come, I'd like to talk about some of the specific challenges posed by Blueprints in MoteMancer, and for hexagons in general, because I'm a nerd and it's fun.

[h3]It's just 60 degree rotations right?[/h3]
In simplest terms, yes, but in practice that's not the starting point that most footprints use. It is important to note that there is a difference between what is mathematically true and what feels correct as game UX. MoteMancer basically has 4 rotation paradigms for the 6 possible directions a building could be in order to make the UX smooth:
[list]
[*] Two rotations - 0° & 60°: we rotate 60 degrees and then rotate back. This is for small buildings like Grindstones.
[*] Two rotations - 0° & 180°: we rotate 180 degrees and then rotate back. This is for larger structures like Titanic Chests and large production structures like a Greenhouse.
[*] Three rotations - 0°, 120°, & 240°: any structure that is symmetric about 180 degrees actually needs 3 rotations to work properly. This applies to things like Wide Chests and Reefcrafters.
[*] All 6 rotations: This applies to Mana Leaves and Streamways.
[/list]
Crucially, while MoteMancer could have used all 6 rotations for every building, it creates a large amount of overhead (6 variants of a building instead of 2), but also means the simple act of rotating would quickly become cumbersome because you would often have to reposition your mouse 2 or 3 times as often because a Structure's rotation point is rarely actually in the exact center, for a myriad of reasons.

[h3]Why does that matter?[/h3]
Once you get to blueprinting and being able to grab multiple structures at a time, now you effectively need to 'teach' each structure what a 60 degree rotation means, even if they don't have one. This is best demonstrated by the image below where a Titanic Chest only has a 0 or 180 degree version. Rotating it 60 degrees intuitively means the pivot should be on the yellow hex, but that pivot orientation doesn't actually exist, the pink dots are the true 'center' coordinate used to place the Structure. So the game has to fake it - telling the Titanic Chest to use its 180° version, but nudging it a hex over so it looks like a 60° rotation.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/3365e9acacb512d633ecb48c4e10aca49df00aec.png[/img]
So in effect you need to make a set of rules for each rotation paradigm, with the added challenge of making sure odd and even rows offset correctly based on the source and destination coordinate. All of the problems are solvable, but come with many mathematical edges that need to be precise.

[h3]And that's just the rotation logic side[/h3]
Beyond the simple math, making sure there are sufficient previews visuals and supporting shaders adds an extra layer of complexity, because not all of MoteMancers structures are handled the same way. Every tile visual like Mana Roots and Streamways have their own suites of tilemaps, and those exist on every plane, so the simple act of doubling those up for the sake of previews is a scary prospect in a game that is performance-sensitive. 

Ultimately I ended up leveraging a similar tech to the Streamway/Shifting Slab join tech - where I am placing an invisible tile reference on their respective maps to fake the neighbor rules.  In this case, I made a completely bespoke set of tiles for preview purposes that can coexist on the same map, which solves One of the problems... but not the other. Since Blueprints and placed Structures are mutually exclusive, I can rely on them to never overlap, but for previewing a placement that is not the case. The preview cursor set itself needs yet another layer of custom logic and shaders, which needs its own set of rules.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/0f1febf6f17a232851dea0a975e25cfada6d0d32.png[/img]

[h3]Sprinkles and the cherry on top[/h3]
After all of that mathemagical wrangling, I’m happy to say Blueprints are in a pretty good spot and [b]will be available with the next update![/b] A fun addition added specifically for MoteMancer is a structure will automatically rotate and snap into position if your cursor matches the blueprint. Not really required in a game where everything is a square, but for a hex grid with unique shapes and 6 rotations, it's a simple quality of life add that feels good. 

The UI has 7 folders designated by elemental icons which can be used literally or in your own mental map way (and can be modded to support more for people that want it). Each folder can hold an unlimited number of blueprints. 

I waffled a lot on whether I would let players share strings with each other, because I feel like a lot of the joy in MoteMancer comes from solving your own spatial problems, and I didn't want people to "net-deck" their factories. That said, I realized my initial hesitation was too rigid and that perfecting blueprints, sharing them, and iterating as a group is its own type of fun. MoteMancer is also thankfully very resilient to being over-solved with blueprints because there are so many different approaches to problems and paths to take to get there. Which is a very long way of saying - blueprints are copyable into strings as you'd expect :)

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/54037ec78f081302d9ae52ac2fe3bb25ea6bc0d7.png[/img]

One last bit about the future of Blueprints - they will be iterated upon with player feedback of course, but one thing I'd like to do is leverage the Research Plane hook that MM uses for walking around the tech tree, and create a sort of Mind Palace for placing blueprints down and tweaking them. This will also lead to tech for sandbox modes in the future, but I will likely focus on making the game more complete before getting into that. Good to already have ideas on where to go from here though, and definitely do share feedback as always.

The Entropy Update will hit experimental in the next day or two for smoke testing, and Live to everyone shortly after. Thanks for all of your support! As always, back to the lab 🌿
~CyanAvatar

notes.title: Monday Musings #24 – Scythe & Spindle - Upcoming Update
notes.content:
I knew at EA launch that Entropy as an adversary would be something that evolved over the course of development, but more than that I also knew I needed feedback to guide the ultimate shape MoteMancer's adversary would take. We've had many late-night community conversations about where we might be able to evolve Entropy, and today I'm going to share the fruits of those discussions.

[h3]Entropy as a Resource[/h3] 
The best way at a foundational level to change the way players interact with Entropy is to make it harvestable and useful rather than just something to carve into or build around. Entropy represents the unraveling of order, thread by thread, into a miasma of noise without enough structure to cohere into anything descript. For an experimenting alchemist, this means it could be leveraged in a multitude of novel and interesting ways.

We'll start with the [b]Entropic Alembic[/b], which distills nearby Entropy into [b]Entropic Shards[/b] - a crystallized reagent used as the foundation of our new arcane endeavors. From there, the [b]Transmutation Engine[/b] channels the chaotic potential of Entropy in a variety of forms. 

Early on, the Engine’s primary use-case is coaxing random Motes back from Entropy using Salt or Aether as a catalyst - reconstituting the Entropic Shard back into that which it dissolved. The random nature of the output adds for interesting logistical challenges, but can also always be turned back into Salt and Aether, since a Grindstone is undiscerning in that regard. Grippers will only pickup Ingredients that are useable in their destination Inventory as well, so there are many clever ways to filter a line, even before Enchanted and Stonebound techs come online. 

Beyond that, the Transmutation Engine allows you to cycle items through their Elemental counterparts. Accidentally bring 100 Streamways to the Fire plane where they can't be placed? Use the Transmutation Engine to convert them into Wide Chests or Ichor Slick, whatever suits your preference.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/130d22700e3c03a4b3620b5443116adcc77c2ac9.png[/img]        [i]Early Entropy Development[/i]

[h3]Inter-Planar Logistics[/h3]
Right now all of the Planar Portals have their cross-plane bridges on all the time, but it was always planned for this to be earned one way or another, and Entropy's kit of slicing through the planes is a perfect place for this tech to unlock. Each Element has its own style of Planar Bridging, and each can be earned through Entropy Research.

Alongside these planar bridges comes a new feature - [b]Planar Reliquary[/b], which allows you to place an in-world "Chest" of sorts that is linked regardless of distance to a reserved slot in your inventory. The easiest use-case for this is to fill it from a Crafter or a line so that you always have a stack of your go-to Structures at hand, but since it lives in the world, it can also be used as a trash slot or canary buffer for whether a supply chain is running low or topped off.

[h3]Spindle & Scythe[/h3]
For players that would rather just prevent Rifts from spawning so they can build in peace - [b]Spindle [/b]is a Diamond-shelled structure that holds a core of Entropy, keeping a local balance and preventing Rifts from reacting to nearby complexity. Spindles effectively stitch the seams of reality together, and has a research line that pushes Entropy back in a variety of ways. [b]Scythe [/b]on the other hand tears reality asunder, concentrating so much abundant Power in a location that a Rift can't help but open to feast on the concordance of energy. Scythe gameplay is about beckoning Entropy into your world so that it may be reaped and exploited.

[h3]Feeding the Cycle[/h3]
Entropy Research is a brand new tech tree that lives alongside the existing elemental tree. Research is simply commenced through cleansing nearby Entropy and Rifts, through Spells or Towers (but notably not through the Entropic Alembic). This gives players a clear path of bonus for killing Rifts, or farming it outright for new avenues of gameplay. There are a few extra goodies buried in the tree, but those you'll have to discover for yourself.

The Entropy Update is encroaching on the horizon - prepare your defenses or distilleries for the dance ahead.

~CyanAvatar

notes.title: Monday Musings #23 – Tips, Tricks, & Tutorials
notes.content:
There's a consistent struggle for any game: how much do you let the player discover for themselves, how much do you tell them, and what if anything do you force them to do? I've always held games like Celeste in high regard for how much the game teaches the player through "Show, don't Tell", but that gets harder and harder to do well as you give the player an increasing amount of actions and freedom.

Sometimes complex games just throw you in the deep end to sink or swim, and I honestly think that's more correct than not. I've always advocated to respect the intelligence of your players. That said, confusion and boredom are the quickest ways to cool your player's enthusiasm, so there is definitely not a one-size-fits-all approach. Add to that the myriad of player psychologies and approaches to solving problems and that's as good an encapsulation of game design challenges as any.

MoteMancer has the extra hurdle of the alchemy skin, since that kit that is not commonly seen in modern media. So with that in mind, MoteMancer's early tutorial deliberately tries to give you as little information as possible, while still guiding you through the important mechanics of the game. This worked to some degree, but it needs improvement, and I'd like to talk through some of the specific areas I've learned from as I've watched players directly or indirectly through comments.

[h3]Logistics Puzzles[/h3]
One of the big critiques I've heard is that "you don't get to the fun fast enough". I think when the game allows you to place Structures anywhere just to see what they do that makes sense, but one of the game's strengths is how logistics puzzles on the hex grid create a novel space for your brain to puzzle in, even in the first few Structures placed. I think that because the player is forced to hand-craft their initial Structures, they are spending more brain cycles on the crafting chain than the logistics puzzle, and I can help them there by providing an objective and a handful of Structures to get started with.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/2fdc3e6b00e9c0dc2634701775552d43a79df289.png[/img]
Even a setup as small as this already has interest - Collectors are 2:1 ratio to Grindstones, they can be setup with a direct output line, and a single Mana Flare can power them all. Most players will start with something like the example on the right, which is perfectly serviceable, but it doesn't prime them for where the joy and interest in the game truly resides. This is a perfect case where a player will probably figure it out eventually, but will a player bounce off the game before they get there? Some for sure, so it's probably worth directly asking them to solve a simple puzzle like "Power 3 Structures with a single Mana Flare" just to get their gears turning.

[h3]Novel Research[/h3]
MoteMancer's research style is not common in automation games, but is also not completely original, many Minecraft mods use Fusion Crafting in one form or another, and this is heavily inspired by that. One of the biggest benefits of this style of research is that it flows back into the logistics puzzle part of the game, where positioning and transport matters just as much as the recipe itself. Despite having an animated gif and examples on the store page, players often don’t stumble onto extra Altar layouts as early as they could, even though it usually delights them once they do.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/afc6b3e688a7e9bfdd78b4b5969c9a56504cdb75.png[/img]
One other thing people don't think of is how Pedestals can act as a simple buffer as well to allow for chaining research like this image on the left. And the right image is a demonstration of either 6 altars researching the same thing, or it could be changed into a hub researching 3 separate things at double speed because Pedestals can share Altars and vice versa. This is another area where simply planting the seed "Have at least 2 Pedestals linked to 2 different Infusion Altars" as an objective points them in a direction of problem solving and fun rather than asking for "A way to speed the game up" because they are just waiting on one Altar to do all the work.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/54037ec78f081302d9ae52ac2fe3bb25ea6bc0d7.png[/img]
The new Entropy Update is fast approaching, and part of that is going to be trying to smooth out the early game tutorials in places like this, as well as making Entropy much more interesting to interact with rather than just being a cleansable area denial. Even the way you first interact with Entropy when you unlock Riptide will change, but I'll save that update for next week.

If you are reading this and have suggestions for other ways to improve the early game tutorialization or "things i wish i knew earlier", I'd be happy to hear them and incorporate them if possible.

Thank you for the ongoing feedback and engagement, MoteMancer is better because of you, keep it coming!
~CyanAvatar

notes.title: Monday Musings #22 – MoteMancer Map Math, Part 2
notes.content:
Part of the reason MoteMancer didn't start with a map is because of how technically challenging it is to juggle hexagons and performance when you aren't working with a standard grid. What does a pixel even mean? Are hexagons expected to match the world? What's the best way to save a texture knowing a bunch of the space is likely to be wasted?

If I'm honest, I was secretly hoping that the in-world compass provided by Seismic Flare and the world flora leading you towards Mote Fields would be enough - there is a magic in the immersion of needing to navigate your world by landmarks alone. But, there are two major design reasons to add a map to MoteMancer:
[list]
[*] The Alchemical foundation of the game is not as intuitive a kit as a standard factory, but it is the conceit for the game and is unlikely to change. This is an important point because there are only so many things a player will bump into before they get too frustrated to continue. While I think the idea of a map-less experience is cool, having both mental burdens forced upon the player early can be too overwhelming.
[*] The world is infinite, so the concept of a land-marker is much harder to latch onto. Because the world is largely self-similar, getting a [i]little [/i]lost can quickly lead to getting [i]very [/i]lost.
[/list]
Also it's one of the most player-requested features, which counts for a lot,

[h3]Always Back to Math[/h3]
So the first idea I had was to fake a half-pixel offset in a resulting map texture using some clever mod-math like this:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/eb3b0d25b9f8ef638d45804b2c33751e2666e286.gif[/img]

Then our forums started discussing ways to get the pixels to look like hexagons, and shared a bunch of super cool shaders that let you do this:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/dbcad563e2cb34bb6d38cce916e975e475800a76.gif[/img]

[h3]And That's When it Fell Apart[/h3]
I spent an entire day trying to get these two methods to play nicely with each other in a variety of ways and always came up [i]just[/i] short of it working. I would either get an extra row here, or the wrong offset value there, it turns out that there's a lot of nuance in the width x height ratio of a hexagonal tiling grid. Mapping an orderly set of squares to that with proper offsets is just one too many balls to juggle.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/e3ea344fabe2413acd37ed48b8641baff05ca267.png[/img]
I won't bore you with all the gory details, but here's a quick graveyard of some of the paths i tried and failed to get there with. I got close from a few different angles, but "close" and "correct" are not the same thing.

[h3]Giving Up?[/h3]
I think it is super important to share when you try something and don't quite make it. It is always a very natural part of the creation process, especially when you are treading territory that is less traveled. I do think that simply offsetting by half a pixel is functional, and already something most people don't do, so is an improvement on just mapping a coordinate system to a square grid.

But........ after stepping away to work on another problem this morning, I received a flash of insight. I am spending an enormous amount of effort effectively trying to procedurally create a set of UVs with very specific values... and I know what the end result should be... which means logically I can just make it by hand. It's not actually that different from making custom Streamway or Grindstone UVs, and since I know exactly what shape/tiling/colors each hex needs to be, a single custom UV texture is all I need. It's definitely a little silly to take a very procedural-feeling thing and hit it with the art hammer, but I guess there's a great lesson in that - If you are a hammer, every problem looks like a nail, changing your tool can change your perspective completely. I was definitely so focused on solving the problem from the engineering angle that I didn't even consider solving it from the art angle.

[h3]Ever Towards the Horizon[/h3]
Every hour spent in game development is opportunity cost, and compartmentalizing this problem to a single day helped me set it down to see the problem from a different angle. While I do have to move on to work on the larger feature I'm planning for an upcoming milestone, I have better perspective for how I'm going to solve this problem in the future (and honestly that could even be tomorrow). For now the player map is functional and I'm certain changing pixels to hexagons will happen in short order. Thanks to everyone for all of the resources and help with solving this problem. Even though I didn't get there, I learned a ton, and gave me enough perspective to find a novel solution that will work.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/df5605e8f0980b1ce434c0ce4b929d26f4117422.png[/img]

The Map still needs a little feature love but should be ready for Thursday's patch. If you want to see all the code snippets I tried, there's a fair few of them in Discord, and I'm sure a procedural solution exists out there if someone is looking for a hard problem to solve for fun :)

Back to the lab!
~CyanAvatar

notes.title: Monday Musings #21 – Working with Bestagons (Part 1)
notes.content:
Hexagons have been a core part of MoteMancer’s design from day one. But knowing I wanted hexes and actually understanding all their nuances are two very different things. Today I want to share a little mathemagical discovery that totally blew my mind and shaped how a lot of MoteMancer works behind the scenes.

[h3]🧩 Rule Tiles and Hexes[/h3]

Unity has a super powerful system called Rule Tiles: you can define how a tile should behave based on its neighbors. There are tons of resources for how to leverage this for square tiles, but very little for hexagons.

When I sat down to map out every possible neighbor combination for a hex tile, something uncanny happened: [b]There are exactly 64 unique combinations.[/b]

Being an FX Artist for years, this was baffling. We often think in atlases and 4x4 or 8x8 grids, so for this to magically manifest as a perfect atlas set immediately made me think i did something wrong. It turns out there is a super well-established reason for this.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/b6dc6b797a6491599974c55340ca91defe0102b5.png[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/54037ec78f081302d9ae52ac2fe3bb25ea6bc0d7.png[/img]
[h3]🔺 Pascal’s Triangle[/h3]

Here’s how all the neighbor connections break down:
[list]
[*] 1 way to have no neighbors.
[*] 1 way to have all 6 neighbors.
[*] 6 ways to have exactly 1 or 5 neighbors.
[*] 15 ways to have exactly 2 or 4 neighbors (two sets of 6 plus the 3 straight sections).
[*] 20 ways to have exactly 3 neighbors (three sets of 6 plus the 2 perfect triangles).
[/list]
And those values are a perfect match to the 6th row of Pascal’s Triangle.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/431ea8ca2ae92fa69c4e9f1676351f36b1125785.png[/img]
That means the humble hex grid is hiding binomial coefficients under the hood, and likely has this pattern for any shape, which is a super fun random math fact that I would never have known. It also demonstrates how much more complex hexes are compared to squares for artistic considerations.


[h3]⚗️ Where it shows up[/h3]

Every omni-directional visual in MoteMancer - Mana Roots, Ichor Slicks, Swiftstone, and more - is built on this foundation. Understanding that there’s an orderly backbone beneath the complexity plays a huge part in how to wield the rule tile system into something predictable and fun to work with.

I’ll dig deeper into the layered nuance that have been built atop this in a future musing, but for now I just wanted to share this little piece of hex-shaped serendipity. Next time you’re laying out your alchemical garden, take a moment to stop and bask in the bestagons.

Back to the lab,
~CyanAvatar

notes.title: Monday Musings #20 – MoteMancer Map Math
notes.content:
MoteMancer has always been about six overlapping planes of existence. From the very start, I knew this meant one big challenge: how do you make overlapping worlds feel harmonious?

At first, I imagined each plane acting on a shared landmass. Raise the seas here, swap water for lava there. Simple idea… but too samey. It robbed each plane of identity. It was way more fun to let Earth become twisting canyons, Water become wide sweeping beaches, Fire become volcanic wastelands. Unique spaces felt much better.

But then came the next problem: how do you ensure unique lands still intersect cleanly at Planar Portals?


[h3]Fibonacci to the Rescue[/h3]

MoteMancer’s world is infinite, so I needed math that could hold up at scale while still feeling organic. I turned to an old favorite: the Fibonacci spiral lattice.

In this image, each dot in the spiral represents a portal combo: Cyan = Life/Water, Magenta = Life/Earth, and so on. It spreads portals evenly without rigid repetition. Because the world was huge, I intuitively added some extra spacing as they drifted further from the center of the world, but more on that later.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/9a5855bb165cfa02c55001d07e1a65cb89febd04.png[/img]


[h3]From Circles to Coastlines[/h3]

Early on, portals just carved out round circles of space. It worked, but it looked… artificial. Too neat. So I added UV noise to the boundaries to breathe life into the coastlines, making them jagged and organic. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/8bf5348282d7a1f9688c1b6417d06f263d813a71.png[/img]

Then I got to leverage some of my favorite math and FX techniques to cast the two relevant portal colors into Red and Green, and leave all the others Blue.
That does three very cool things:
[olist]
[*] [b]Shaping coastlines[/b] – Red and green areas deform terrain to make room for portals, while blue areas keep the coastline natural.
[*] [b]Hidden knowledge[/b] – Blue marks also quietly reveal where a portal exists in another plane. If you notice it, you feel like you’ve uncovered an easter egg.
[*] [b]Terrain Texture Masking[/b] – This elegantly allows a single terrain material to treat each color as both a heightmap and mask for multiple textures, allowing them to not only blend organically into each other, but also gives a clear space for things like near-portal tiles and biomes.
[/olist]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/6e8403e9e9c8bdb107b8cb31047d10e7b7506373.png[/img]

[h3]Seeds, Bugs, and Feedback[/h3]

The entire game runs on procedural generation, but I locked the seed early for two reasons:

[olist]
[*] Player feedback – I originally thought portals should spread further apart the further you go. But in practice, since you only ever see two per plane at once, the distances were already big enough. Feedback convinced me to tighten the spiral back up for better pacing.
[*] Bug hunting – Cloud saves revealed a wild GPU quirk where different hardware actually generated slightly different coastlines. Same seed, different shapes. Locking the world made it easier to isolate the problem so it can be addressed before the flood gates open.
[/olist]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/cae49996c4251ce7036080fa955f0db2e500bc81.png[/img]

And that’s the real win: the math foundation was solid, but the community made it better.

Big thanks to everyone who explored deep into the infinite terrain and stress-tested this system across hardware. Every bug report and suggestion has helped me sculpt a world that feels strange, magical, and infinite. World seeds are just a hop skip and a jump away. There are a few optimizations to be made alongside moving the algorithm from GPU to CPU, and I want to make sure that saves are backwards compatible. Almost there :)

See you on the planes,
~CyanAvatar

notes.title: Monday Musings #19 - Community Spotlight!
notes.content:
I've always loved games where players can set their own goals and fulfill them creatively - there's lovely freedom that comes from setting an ambitious project for yourself and seeing it though piece by piece. MoteMancer always had tiling patterns and interesting shapes in mind as part of the joy and personalization of base building. I always imagined that instead of bases looking like circuit boards as they do on a traditional grid, they might look more like a Mandala or stained-glass window on a hex grid.

The thing about bases in games like this, is your base is often just as much your 'character' as the alchemist running around. It's a trail of breadcrumbs because [i]you[/i] placed every single item, made every single decision, and it feels like home. Today I'd love to shine a bit of a spotlight on the many creative ways the community has tended their automagical gardens, showing off the diversity of thought, playstyle, and techniques used to grapple with the hexagonal tetris that is MoteMancer.

So without further ado, here are just a small handful of amazing designs from our community:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/54037ec78f081302d9ae52ac2fe3bb25ea6bc0d7.png[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/f9c0dafe4c4edc89e2d770c6481a6e54e6373664.png[/img]
I want to start with this shot from [i]According-Studio-658[/i] because it's a great shot of bases from both the Earth and Life planes at once. There are many unique techniques used here like the choice between single and double 'vertical' lines, radial power generation, simple mall setups, and a clear progression of understanding the game's building language. Wonderful shot.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/89a458aa7fe836c07f24e781035f31d77dbc0704.png[/img]
This compilation from [i]Wempi_01[/i], [i]vonBoomslang[/i], [i]taronin[/i], and [i]Vazhi [/i]shows 4 completely different approaches to using Tidal Collectors. They each speak for themselves, and are a wonderful demonstration of how many ways you can choose to solve spatial problems, even on something as simple as resource collection.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/2b1603ba60f04c50cad00f0044fe7fb2f4df339f.png[/img]
[i]Syuushi [/i]is our resident mall builder, and it was hard picking out a specific shot because there are so many to choose from, but I always appreciate the time put in to not just be functional but aesthetic. I look forward to seeing more designs as more pathways are added to the game and more building animations bring the malls to life.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/655682deb98fd89a95fcbfd3b3375507d4a7ffb4.png[/img]
I love [i]Gibli's [/i]mix of Ichor Slick and Torrential Streamways here. Ichor Slicks are fairly late game if you have not seen them yet, and cannot be adjacent to each other like a Streamway or Shifting Slab can be. This base does a superb job of keeping the logistics separated by organized, all while keeping a harmonious vibe.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/5b977a39018a62264acb953531c97a4a5c308a72.png[/img]
[i]zoycite [/i]has done much work to pioneer functional and aesthetic Earth Chest setups - too many to even show here, but these are some of my favorites. I appreciate the time taken to just make something cool for cool's sake, especially since you'll run by it another dozen or hundred times over the course of your playthrough, and will be a constant source of joy.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/5fd10497de81df3d97b70e50556bb4460871f652.png[/img]
[i]Tenebrais[/i] has a lovely shot of a fire base at night, alight with Fire Wire and Collector crystals. Honestly when I look at this shot I'm reminded of how much work I want to do to improve the night time visuals in MoteMancer - Emberboughs and Shadefangs should glow, Ichor needs some galactic vibes. Those will all come in time, but gameplay still takes precedent for now :)


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/c14b1c0211bbfc0cc10cf24eaa35e55c61284d1c.png[/img]
[i]falk[/i] has too many builds to show (and also streams! check it out!), but this is one of my favorites. Even though there was a lighting bug on streams and pathways that I cannot unsee (and has since been fixed), this design is still awesome to look at. I look forward to many more functional and aesthetic creations to come.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/b292d19f9d7011fc74efea53b6ce492ad87dd892.png[/img]
I love this base from [i]nnelg[/i], there are 3 specific things that stand out for me: I love the repeated theme of elemental binders, definitely a reminder that the game needs blueprints; I love that there are still a few ad-hoc areas that needed to 'just work'; but most of all i love that there are clearly manicured trees and bushes set in areas that could only be done by Nudging the doodads into place. Well done on all counts :)


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/5110e209f3c346bcd05bd6f7037fa908cd20dbab.png[/img]
In this build, [i]Salty Minstrel[/i] truly embraces the 'pool' aspect of Ichor Slick. While you can treat Ichor like a traditional belt in a lot of ways, it also has incredible use-cases for being whatever shape you want as long as you can keep the pools separate. I'm so happy Ichor is landing in the clear arc of "I don't get it", "Oh that's interesting", "Holy crap this is powerful". An analogy floating around the community is to think of Ichor Slick as a 'paintable Chest', and I think that description is very apt.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/54037ec78f081302d9ae52ac2fe3bb25ea6bc0d7.png[/img]

There are so many more designs that I could show off, definitely join our discord and reddit to see more of the amazing creativity rampant in the community. It's wonderful to build a sandbox for people, and then see all the ways they use their toys to build their own personal castles. I think I'm going to start using people's builds as capsules for devlogs going forward because there's so much to share :)

The factory gardens must grow,
[i]~CyanAvatar[/i]

notes.title: Monday Musings #18 - Runeshroom Rituals
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/54037ec78f081302d9ae52ac2fe3bb25ea6bc0d7.png[/img]

One of the most beloved Minecraft mods I ever played was Astral Sorcery. Drawing massive constellations from the night sky onto your Attunement Altar to bind yourself to the stars... it was a powerful blend of mechanical progression and pure fantasy flavor. Even though it gave way to a traditional talent tree, the fantasy was just spectacular.

MoteMancer is definitely inspired by a variety of those beloved mods, and tries to build something new and interesting on those foundations, which leads us to Runeshroom Rituals.

[h3]Grounding the System[/h3]
MoteMancer’s design has a few guiding pillars, and one of the big ones is this:
Every space should have an opportunity cost.

That means the idea of placing a constellation on the ground where the 'stars' take up precious building space is a perfect fit. You build a ritual by laying out caps (like Flamecap, Shadecap, or Cloudcap) in a specific runic shape. That shape then generates an area effect. And because caps take up space, the structures you want to benefit from the ritual have to work around them. It follows the DNA of MoteMancer - always granting you a benefit through a spatial puzzle.

[h3]Influence and Function[/h3]
Rituals in MoteMancer are like beacons from previous games, buffing affected structures or even just the area itself within. Rituals cannot overlap each other, but a single structure can sit at the intersection of three separate rituals. If any part of a structure is inside a ritual's area, it gains the benefit. This encourages clever layout strategies and leads to satisfying, emergent solutions.

Shadow structures in particular are designed with this in mind. Their long, winding shapes can thread between mushroom caps in ways others can't. It fits perfectly with Shadow’s theme of subtlety and slipping between the seen and unseen. Also since Blazecaps and Cloudcaps have dual element associations, they follow the same Planar exclusivity that other combo buildings do, so your strategy will shift as it always has depending on the Elemental Plane you find yourself in.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/57254b9d79025854b05258e861a14f150c1072db.png[/img]
[h3]Current Rituals[/h3]
Here are the rituals planned so far:

[b]Echocatcher [/b]– 10% chance to duplicate a Structure’s output.
[b]Shadeveil [/b]– Prevents Entropy from spreading into the area.
[b]Darkreach [/b]– Removes all Reach restrictions within the Ritual.

[b]Windshear [/b]– Amplifies open-air tiles inside the ritual. 
[b]Tailwind [/b]– Boosts crafting speed of all Structures inside.

[b]Emberheart [/b]– Reduces Mana cost of nearby Structures.
[b]Amplify [/b]– Each Lava tile inside increases Lava Generator Heat.

[h3]Open Design Space[/h3]
There is still (at least) one open ritual slot for Fire and Air - so if you have cool ideas, I’d love to hear them! There are a lot of opportunities to use Runeshroom Rituals for Tower benefits, or maybe even some sort of Chasm gameplay. The original two I had planned are not cool enough, we can do better :)

The best part of Rituals is they don’t eat into a Production Structure's recipe limit, so they don’t compete for their slot the way brand new Structures do. There's even a possibility for other elemental combinations later if there's a cool enough thing to chase.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/54037ec78f081302d9ae52ac2fe3bb25ea6bc0d7.png[/img]

It started with a love of constellations.
It ended in a field of mushrooms.
And I couldn’t be happier.

Blazecap and Cloudcap will be in Thursday's build! I can't wait to see what grows :) 
~CyanAvatar

notes.title: Monday Musings #17 - Making Games to be Made, not just Played.
notes.content:
One of the most lasting lessons from AAA is that iteration is everything. If you want to make something good, you have to be able to keep making it. So for MoteMancer, it was never just about building the final game, it was about building the game in a way that was enjoyable and fast to iterate on.

From day one, I asked:
[b]“How can I make this game easy and fun to make?”[/b]

Before I wrote a single system, I blocked out the core data I’d need, and how I'd want to edit it. This image is many years old, well before a single line of code was written, just exploring how I'd want to edit the game:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/5a1d2abeb3d88362701cb7982eb254887c77fafb.png[/img]
[list]
[*] Entity – A thing you carry or transport around
[*] Structure – A thing you place and interact with
[*] Footprint – The shape a Structure occupies
[*] Recipe – How inputs become outputs
[*] Resource – What exists in the world (now “Mote Fields”)
[/list]
These interfaces have evolved greatly over the course of development, but it's important to show how unrefined early games truly are. These concepts are still the beating heart of the game, and they’re the reason bugs are fast to fix and iteration is fun. A wise mentor once told me [i]"Game Dev = Bugs."[/i] Never a truer equation was uttered. Thus, setting myself up for future success became ever-present mindset.

[h3]Designing for Future-You[/h3]
If a task isn’t trivial, I spend time first making it trivial. Not with bulletproof systems, just with directional tools. I ask:  [b]“Is there a future pain point I can reduce right now?”[/b]

That principle doesn’t just apply to gamedev. It applies to cooking, leatherworking - any craft where your skill improves by improving your process. Half the joy is in making the next attempt smoother than the last. When your tools are not getting in your way you spend more time in flow state, perfecting the craft itself.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/6c195b01cd92ccb8fe1ee219da5a746dc1ad9d34.png[/img]

[h3]My Favorite Button in the World[/h3]
Most of MoteMancer’s tuning data doesn’t live in-engine. It lives in a spreadsheet, where I can balance everything side-by-side. Recipes, research, and localization all gets pushed into Unity with one click.

That one-click philosophy scales up, too:
[list]
[*] Import tuning from Excel
[*] Import multi-language localization
[*] Build every platform - Demo, Full, (soon to include Linux and Mac)
[*] Push to Steam
[/list]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/3da0aff250f658dab88dc7578bbe989a045829db.png[/img]
All from one button.

These individually took about a day each to build. They’ve repaid themselves a hundred times over - not just in time saved, but in flow protected. When you’re not interrupted by tedium, your focus is easier to maintain, which also pays for itself in spades.

[h3]My Guiding Rule[/h3]
Here’s the guiding principle that’s kept me sane:
[i]If it’s not trivial, spend 30–60 minutes making it more trivial. Then do the thing.[/i]

Don’t overbuild. Don’t chase the perfect editor. Make the main things trivial, medium things easier, and everything else sane.

This is likely not the first time you've seen or heard advice like this. In my experience, sometimes you just need to hear it from another perspective to remember that your time is worth investing in. Hopefully this sparks something for your own project. I'm certain the time I've spent writing this and you've spent reading this will likewise pay for itself many times over :)

—
Stay savvy, MoteMancers.
~CyanAvatar

notes.title: Monday Musings #16 - Towards the Horizon Together
notes.content: [p]First of all - Thank You for an amazing EA launch week. The community response has been everything I'd hoped for and more, and I'm so looking forward to continuing to develop the game with and for our growing menagerie of MoteMancers.[/p][p][/p][p]I want to be up front with what to expect in the coming weeks and months - MoteMancer still has tons of polish and features and quality of life to implement, but the game is largely stable, and that changes our development posture a little bit. Where patches were coming in almost daily leading up to launch and through last week, that cadence is likely to drop to about once a week.  My current plan is to keep doing [b]Monday Musings[/b] and then push a more robust [b]patch every Thursday[/b]. [/p][p][/p][p]One of the immediate things I'm going to tackle is doing a large Localization QA pass - I think the translation itself is great (please continue to give feedback where you find ways to improve it) - but there are definitely areas where there are awkward line breaks and some UI's that got missed, and I want to shore all of that up as a priority.[/p][p][/p][p]After that there will be a big push for additional Quality of Life and UX, in addition to getting many of the fractured researches available that didn't quite make it in time for Automation Fest. Finding a balance is definitely going to be part of the challenge - as with all game development, the more consistently a feature or fix is requested, the higher priority it will be. I'm confident that we can keep a good clip of updates, and the main challenge is going to be where to channel our focus.[/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/54037ec78f081302d9ae52ac2fe3bb25ea6bc0d7.png"][/img][/p][p]But I don't want to end there. I want to end with one of my favorite story arcs that happened last week for those that missed it - proving for always and eternity that players will find ways to surprise you.[/p][p][/p][p]This is the tale of [b]Ellensiel[/b], the MoteMancer who stayed behind.[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/0f3ae63c5300ea3743ffc9d926f11d4e93b8a97d.png"][/img][/p][p]Refusing to surrender, Ellensiel chose to remain in the Library, determined to fight the encroaching threat of Entropy from within. The resources for apprenticeship after-all remained within the great hall. As instructed, Salt and Aether foundations were swiftly established, giving way to the Element of Life revealing itself. [/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/ce8a5f8e4d85fdad0d77a8250f9cab2afeca77ac.png"][/img][/p][p]In spite of the valiant effort, resources were running shallow, and the Elemental Orbs would require significantly more coalesced elemental essence to be reformed. Undeterred, Ellensiel found more and more nuanced tactics to leverage the tools available, cleverly threading Shifting Slabs beneath the ominous Rifts. [/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/75da994a0336ff9a29238bb39d62ea5dcf123664.png"][/img][/p][p]Such masterful order created a stronger counterbalance from the nearby Rifts, seeking to nullify the local pocket of complexity. Ellensiel, having learned much while remaining in the library, narrowly slipped through the portal to the Life Plane - seeking a way to restore the Elemental Orbs, and preserve the fragile middle, where creation renews itself against the flattening calm of Entropy.[/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/54037ec78f081302d9ae52ac2fe3bb25ea6bc0d7.png"][/img][/p][p][/p][p]Thank you Ellensiel for the joy of crawling around the rough edges of MoteMancer, I look forward to continually being surprised :)[/p][p][/p][p][i]~Cyanavatar[/i][/p][p][/p][p][/p][p][/p][p][/p]

notes.title: Monday Musings #15 - MoteMancer Early Access starts today!
notes.content: [h3]Greetings Automagical Alchemists,[/h3][p][/p][p]MoteMancer has been years in development, and while there is still plenty left to build, I can think of nothing more fitting than releasing into [b]Early Access[/b] with [b]Automation Fest[/b] along-side the giants that have inspired me to make this game.[/p][p][/p][p]I'd like to share a roadmap (also available in game) of where MoteMancer is heading, and give some context around the simplified concepts to share my headspace. [/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/170589ab5b93742e54c538961ac03023707aa6bb.png"][/img][/p][p][b]Research[/b] - While the research tree is vast, there is still plenty of room for improvement and additions. Some slots you see in the research tree are Shattered, typically consisting of plans already thought out for the future, but also an opportunity for the community to take existing ideas and either make them better or outright replace them.  [/p][p][/p][p][b]Air and Fire Power[/b] are hot off the press - they are very different from Life and also the least tested, so I imagine there will be improvements to be made there, but there are already interesting synergy and logistics nuances to each.[/p][p][/p][p][b]Runeshrooms[/b] will be later in your journey as they are Tier 2 Shadow research, but they offer a unique take on beacon gameplay, heavily inspired from Astral Sorcery. Currently there are two rituals available but 9 are planned.[/p][p][/p][p][b]Spell Improvements[/b] - Some spells deeper in the tree are not yet implemented but also some of the original ideas made less sense. There are also ways to improve the current spells planned like AoE Nudge and Excavator.[/p][p][/p][p][b]Entropy[/b] itself is a tricky beast, it's very easy to make it too oppressive, so I imagine there will be a lot of feedback in both the tuning of it and the evolution of how the challenge and tension escalates.[/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/fe8efc56a55096b5cb1a1b845214b48338e15463.png"][/img][/p][p][/p][p][b]Blueprints[/b] (and a map) are hot community asks right now. They are both planned and both a little more tricky on a hex grid than a conventional square one, but we'll make it happen :)[/p][p][/p][p][b]Full Controller Support[/b] - technically MoteMancer is already fully playable on Steam Deck - if you are looking for controller layouts there are some floating around out community already. That said, my standards for "Full Support" are very high and i want to make the game very natural to play with a controller, and that will take dedicated time.  The framework is there, but I'm sure you'll agree that nuance and feel are everything for a feature like this.[/p][p][/p][p][b]More Music Tracks![/b] Aleksandria continues to work hard at polishing and refining the existing score, and there are still more tracks in store to round out the planes.[/p][p][/p][p][b]Art Improvements[/b] - There is so much to do here. I think MoteMancer is already in a good state but it could be much better. I have a lot of plans for FX and Night-time visuals especially, but gameplay was more important to focus on before polishing all of that. My hope is that I can spend time working on quality of life and aesthetics while gathering information for the best way to proceed with the larger features.[/p][p][/p][p][b]UI/UX improvements[/b] - Ongoing for sure. People still get stuck at some tutorial moments because the rules are nuanced. For anyone reading this that does get stuck and has an "aha" moment after, sharing what would have made the message more clear for you is [i]suuuuuper[/i] helpful. Send an in-game report with \[F1] and I'll see it.[/p][p][/p][p][b]Affix Modes[/b] - MoteMancer is uniquely positioned for replay-ability because of the structure of the game. What if you started on the Fire Plane and Earth was completely shattered? What if Entropy spawned near every resource patch but Collectors were twice as efficient? There are so many ways to mix and match modifiers for gameplay, and I'm hoping institutionalizing a "Challenge Run" will give MoteMancer immense replayability.[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/06dafa33f06ba05e43fbb27a149e9c4576da70bb.png"][/img][/p][p][b]Infinite Research[/b] - Once the Elemental Orbs are restored, securing a stronger elemental link to the Library will amplify your efficiency in a variety of ways.[/p][p][/p][p][b]Achievements and World Seeds[/b] - Much of this framework is in place, but making the game stable was a top priority. These will come very soon.[/p][p][/p][p]And of course [b]Community Requests[/b] - the in game feedback/bug/suggestion form is the best way to get a message to me at the moment. Hearing thoughts during flow state are super useful. Many ideas have already been implemented, and many more are on the docket.  This game will only get better with your feedback and ideas. [/p][p][/p][p]Also! Any feedback about [b]Localization[/b] is super helpful. MoteMancer definitely has less grounding in reality and I spent a lot of time trying to be poetic and functional and evocative all at the same time, but it's a fine needle to thread and especially in other languages. Any feedback on either syntax or even reading size is very welcome.[/p][p][/p][p][/p][p]There is so much more to do, but the elemental sandbox is already brimming with toys for you to experiment with. Thank you for being along for the journey. And now... back to the lab![/p][p][/p][p][i]~Cyanavatar[/i][/p][p][/p][p][/p][p][/p][p][/p]

notes.title: Monday Musings #14 – Lessons Through Research
notes.content:
[p]As we approach Early Access, I’ve been reflecting on how Research has evolved in MoteMancer, particularly when it comes to Infusion Altar space and ingredient management. Early on, I was well aware of how the novel research design of altars and pedestals came at the cost of space efficiency - you aren't just piping ingredients in like any other structure. So I wanted find ways for research to be space-efficient and allow for shared ingredients across altars to be paramount. Two ingredients felt like a sweet spot where you can have one central shared ingredient and share between 3 corners of nearby altars. And that worked well enough, but...[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/ecd6eb83e510473753a5fc5136b9dac7befb636a.png"][/img][/p][p]Of course, there’s a tradeoff. The tooltips sort of imply that the player should constantly swap ingredients. Even though this wasn't necessarily true in practice (you can just add a third pedestal), I realized the game wasn’t explicitly teaching that as part of the flow.[/p][p][/p][p]After letting it bake for a few months with a lot of testing and feedback, we're reverting back to our original design: branches now add ingredient requirements instead of replacing them. This subtly encourages adding more pedestals to keep things flowing, while making the research tree feel more natural. Instead of the mental two-step of swapping and removing, players simply add, making the experience smoother overall. This also helps encourage the factory to grow, which of course, it must.[/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/b6a1226e5d4fd36c2497d7ec89108f8d4212f7b3.png"][/img][/p][p]And as for research throughput? Turns out, it’s less of a concern than I anticipated. Since you can set up an ad-hoc Altar site anywhere and alters still share 4 sides naturally, players can scale their research in creative ways - both functionally and aesthetically.[/p][p][/p][p]We’re just a week out from Early Access, and while there’s still a lot to build, the foundations are set. There’s plenty to explore, and I can’t wait to see where this journey takes us.[/p][p][/p][p][/p][p]Catch you on the Elemental Planes,
~CyanAvatar[/p]

notes.title: Monday Musings #13 – Entropy Awakens
notes.content: [p]One of the things that struck me playing automation games with adversaries is that when the enemy destroys your structures or kills you, it can feel antithetical to the core loop. That said, enemies serve a valuable purpose: they interfere with your plans.[/p][p][/p][p][b]Entropy[/b] in MoteMancer is my attempt to walk that tightrope—to throw a wrench in the works [i]without[/i] erasing your hard-earned progress. It doesn't kill you. It doesn't destroy your buildings. Instead, it saps the Power from your structures, shutting them down under a spreading miasmic mist.[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/c8edcde5d9ec66225960b144307dbd6464d5be44.png"][/img][/p][p]Importantly, dynamic Entropy doesn't activate until you've passed into your first Plane. Life is meant to be your safe zone and place to learn comfortably. But once you venture further, the inevitability of Entropy begins to catch up with you.[/p][p][/p][p]It starts small. Stir up a Mote Field too much, and a [b]Rift[/b] forms. From it, Entropy spills out. You can ignore it if you like. You can build around it. But it will eat into your build space, and it will grow, ever-creeping. [/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/cb49fe7d95cc1b43b3821bfbe1e7d83b4a372fde.png"][/img][/p][p]Spells can temporarily clear it. But they don’t last. The only lasting solution lies in two Towers:[/p][list][*][p][b]Downpour Bastion[/b] rains down cleansing water, holding the line for the cost of some Elemental Water.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Incineration Spire[/b] burns the Rift closed, halting the spread—but it demands a surge of Power, and any delay means leftover Entropy to clean.[/p][/*][/list][p]Both towers have upgrades. [b]Scorched Earth[/b], for example, turns sealed Rifts into Motes of Fire. You'll need every trick you can muster, because Entropy escalates with each new Plane you visit. It becomes the ultimate plate-spinning act as you fight to restore the Great Portal.[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/41162f03649e7f2036b772373f24d1341d6332fe.png"][/img][/p][p]And the twist: Entropy pierces through Planes. A jostled Mote Field in one Plane might open a Rift that disables part of your base on another. That makes [i]where[/i] you choose to fight it a strategic decision, both spatially and given your access to resources.[/p][p][/p][p]Entropy is MoteMancer's take on a true automation antagonist. It won't break your base. But it will bend your plans. And I can't wait to keep evolving it with your feedback.[/p][p]~CyanAvatar[/p]

notes.title: 🎴 Monday Musings #12 - A Deck of Surprises
notes.content:
[p]Making randomness feel good is one of the trickiest things in games. If you go with true randomness — pure chaos with a side of regret — it often feels terrible to players. It’s clumpy, swingy, and frustrating. Drawing a 1-in-100 result three times in a row isn’t just unlikely — it’s inevitable given enough time, and that kind of streak tends to wreck pacing and fun.[/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/6d00f4ad4e456bc729a284411bfea27857a9577d.png"][/img][/p][p][i]credit: [url="https://forums.lindale.io/t/grid-and-uniform/1154"]https://forums.lindale.io/t/grid-and-uniform/1154[/url][/i][/p][p][/p][p]What players tend to want isn’t “random” — it’s more about “unpredictability.” Something they can’t quite script, but can still react to and reason about. And that’s where my favorite randomization tool comes in: [b]the humble deck of cards.[/b][/p][p][/p][h3]🎲 Why Not Just Roll Dice?[/h3][p]There are all kinds of clever techniques for smoothing out randomness: escalating chances, rerolls, weighted sampling, averaging multiple rolls — and they all work in different contexts. But none of them quite do what a deck of cards does: ensure [i]coverage[/i]. You’ll see every card eventually, but in a shuffled order. Repeats are rare, patterns are broken, and you always get a fresh mix.[/p][p][/p][p]In board games this is standard, but digital games often forget how powerful it can be. In [b]MoteMancer[/b], we use this technique somewhere you might not expect: the music selection system.[/p][p][/p][h3]♠️ Decks Within Decks[/h3][p]Each Element (Life, Earth, Water, etc.) has its own shuffled “deck” of music tracks. When a track plays, it gets set aside until it is ready to be shuffled, and we are guaranteed to not hear it again until we’ve cycled through the rest. Already, this means few repeats, smoother transitions, and way more variety.[/p][p][/p][p]But, we also have a [i]deck of elements[/i] layered on top — like a meta-deck that controls which plane's deck we draw from. It includes cards like “Current Plane”, “Clockwise Plane”, and “Counterclockwise Plane.” Shuffle it, draw one, and use that to pick which elemental deck to pull a track from — using the player's current plane as the key. This technique is affectionately known as a "Deck of Decks".[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/82880201c24470c7f3a7ae9421ff19e978d0c44f.png"][/img][/p][p][/p][p]The result? You always get music that’s relevant to your surroundings, but never in a fixed or looping order. As you move from Life to Water to Air, the soundscape shifts with you — organically and unpredictably, but always feels correct.[/p][p]
[/p][h3]🌱 Predictable Chaos[/h3][p]There are so many more ways to play with this kind of layered randomness. Enemy spawns, game modifiers, even procedural terrain (looking forward to that one!). But for now, I just wanted to highlight a quiet corner of MoteMancer where a bit of clever math makes the world feel alive.[/p][p][/p][p]Thanks for reading, and if you’re curious: yes, I have spreadsheets for all of it. 😇[/p][p][i]~CyanAvatar[/i][/p]

notes.title: Monday Musings #11 – The Winding Road
notes.content: [h2][b]MoteMancer enters Early Access on July 14th[/b]  [/h2][h2][i]as part of Automation Fest![/i][/h2][p]This week marks a big milestone: what began as a solo project, scribbled together from FX tricks and a healthy dose of mathemagic, has grown from a passion project into a full-fledged experience — with dozens of hours of brain-bending gameplay.[/p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/54037ec78f081302d9ae52ac2fe3bb25ea6bc0d7.png"][/img][h3]🌿 Looking Back, and Forward[/h3][p]Next Fest just wrapped, and I can't help but take a moment to look back at where this all began. MoteMancer started as a solo project just because I loved the genre and wanted to learn C#. I think it's important to continually remind players and aspiring developers that everything starts with humble beginnings, and one of my personal goals has always been to inspire future creators and dreamers as I have been inspired. [/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/0d368dc51025dfd4c985463a0c01d9ab6e435ed2.png"][/img][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/54037ec78f081302d9ae52ac2fe3bb25ea6bc0d7.png"][/img][/p][p][/p][h3]💡Continued Creativity[/h3][p]If you missed the streams, check out the replays: [url="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IkP4f8RXgRs"]\[Day 1][/url], [url="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iV8xTkbScjU"]\[Day 2][/url], [url="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vdn6ceOJ628"]\[Day 3][/url], [url="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W6L87Yuy-xc"]\[Day 4][/url].[/p][p]My favorite day by far was showcasing the clever and creative builds dreamt up by the community. MoteMancer is a sandbox with rare rules, encouraging you to think sideways (sometimes literally) and challenge your sense of efficiency and aesthetics consistently. [/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/f3bd409481a47a61abf5364002be584efa1eb542.png"][/img][/p][p]Beyond in-game builds themselves, the community has also contributed some of the best new ideas and features to MoteMancer, notably [b]Rampant Bloom[/b] and [b]Charged Lodestone[/b] were born directly from community feedback. [/p][p]If that’s any indication of what’s to come, we’re in good hands.[/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/54037ec78f081302d9ae52ac2fe3bb25ea6bc0d7.png"][/img][/p][p][/p][h3]🧪 What Comes Next[/h3][p]Early Access is just the next chapter. The game is deep, intricate, and full of promise — but still growing. We’ll continue to fix bugs, add polish, and expand the world with your help. [/p][p]If you haven’t yet: [/p][p]👉 Play the free demo [/p][p]👉 Wishlist MoteMancer for July [/p][p]👉 Join our Discord and be part of the conversation[/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/54037ec78f081302d9ae52ac2fe3bb25ea6bc0d7.png"][/img][/p][p][/p][h3]🌞 Thank You[/h3][p]Seriously — thank you. For every build shared, bug spotted, suggestion posted, and kind word offered. We’re just getting started. See you July 14th for Early Access — and a clear roadmap for what lies ahead. [/p][p][/p][p][i]~CyanAvatar[/i][/p]

notes.title: Monday Musings #9 – Research, Reimagined
notes.content:
In many games, research is a button. You click it, wait, and something unlocks. MoteMancer's research captures the essence of alchemical tinkering through a garden of reagents ready to bloom.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/77b7f48b703562e282dbf1287c42d2ed95d54fe5.png[/img]
[h3]🌟 The Promise of Research[/h3]
To an alchemist, knowledge isn’t bought with time. It’s coaxed out of the world — one reaction at a time. In MoteMancer, you don’t pick a tech from a menu. You fuse a myriad of reagents together to understand their deeper nature and potential.

Every advancement comes from combining elemental ingredients at an [b]Infusion Altar[/b], an homage to fusion crafting traditions seen in many beloved Minecraft Mods like Botania, Ars Nouveau, or Thaumcraft. But instead of scripted rituals, you’re free to place reagents on linked [b]Pedestals [/b]in whatever way suits your imagination, channeling elemental energy through aesthetical inspiration, and creative planning.

[h3]🧪 A System that Grows With You[/h3]
Most early discoveries only require a few components. But as your needs grow, so does your setup. Every Infusion Altar supports up to 18 Pedestals, which can be shared across multiple Altars—and vice versa.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/229b26b0b1e7e5c3bdf3e6da31a838edd923e9a4.png[/img]

This creates a modular puzzle playground:
[list]
[*] Align Altars in a triangle and share a core component across all three
[*] Tile out a modular research garden and share your efficiency masterpiece with the community
[*] Build anywhere — not just a central hub
[/list]
It’s research that bends to your style, not the other way around.

[h3]💡 Speed, Scale, and Serendipity[/h3]
Because every research is item-based, you’re never locked to just one advancement at a time.
Want to push harder on Life tech? Automate Leaves and Life Prisms and flood your Altar with discoveries. Want to prep for future projects? No need to stop your previous research, you can build out the infrastructure to uncover Earth research in tandem.

And when you’ve unlocked the secrets of a given reagent, your automation setup will continue to provide the vital structures that keeps fueling your progress. You’ve earned it.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/dee7731ff7f6ec64beac81eeedb2f9e714c574e1.png[/img]

[h3]🌱 Discovery Will Take Root with Time[/h3]
We know the learning curve for research is a little steeper than most, we know it’s different.  
That’s okay. The joy of MoteMancer is in the personal journey of discovery and knowledge, 
and the research system itself is no exception.

Once it clicks, you'll find yourself dreaming up altar blueprints and crafting layouts in your sleep.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45567834/1893805531fa34bb986ea8a4639fe86e7be90680.png[/img]

Thanks for reading! We'll see you next Monday for another MoteMancer Musing.
Until then, keep those Altars fusing. ✨

[b]~CyanAvatar[/b]
